headline: Xbox charges 24-40 cents/hour to stream games you own, even without Game Pass
summary: Xbox is rolling out 'Cloud Playtime' purchases to Insiders, allowing non-subscribers to stream owned games for an additional hourly fee, starting at 24 cents.
details: Microsoft has rolled out "Cloud Playtime" purchases to Xbox Insiders, allowing non-subscribers to stream eligible games they own. This new a la carte system charges players an additional fee on top of the game's purchase price, with introductory rates ranging from 24 to 40 cents per hour. Purchased playtime hours do not expire.

This model differs significantly from the Xbox Game Pass subscription, which includes limited monthly streaming access to hundreds of games. Unlike Game Pass, these Cloud Playtime packs explicitly require a cloud-playable game purchase or free-to-play access, meaning users pay twice for the same game.

The metered approach evokes old arcade models but contrasts with modern all-you-can-play home experiences. It also differs from Google's Stadia, which offered unlimited streaming for purchased games, and Sony's initial PlayStation Now, which charged for rental periods before shifting to a subscription.

Xbox Insiders can also test free, ad-supported streams of owned games, but Microsoft indicates that paid users will benefit from shorter wait times and higher-quality streaming. This suggests a potentially degraded experience for those opting for the free tier.

The move raises questions about the market for standalone Xbox Cloud Streaming. Microsoft previously noted that only 4% of Game Pass subscribers were affected by new streaming limits, suggesting a small minority heavily uses the cloud feature. It remains to be seen how many non-subscribers will pay hourly for games they already own.

headline_marked: [[Airbnb bans guests from doing chores]] like dishes and stripping beds, sparking host outrage
headline: Airbnb bans guests from doing chores like dishes and stripping beds, sparking host outrage
summary: Airbnb's new policy, effective November 20, prohibits hosts from requiring guests to perform cleaning tasks typically done by a cleaner, leading to significant backlash from hosts.
details: Airbnb has implemented a new policy, effective for bookings made on or after November 20, that bans hosts from requiring guests to complete tasks typically performed by a cleaner. This includes chores like stripping beds, taking out trash, or washing and putting away dishes.

The announcement, sent via email to hosts, immediately sparked outrage within the host community. Many expressed frustration online about losing control over their property's upkeep and feeling unprotected.

Hosts voiced concerns on official forums and Reddit, with some describing Airbnb as an "abusive partner" and threatening to unlist properties or strip kitchens down to bare essentials. They argue they have a responsibility to protect their investments.

Conversely, many guests are celebrating the change, having long complained about paying high cleaning fees while still being required to perform extensive chores. Guests often felt the experience had become "total ass."

Airbnb clarifies that hosts cannot circumvent the policy by listing cleaning tasks in the "Requests" section or by requiring guests to sign separate contracts. The platform's interface now actively prevents such requests from being saved.

Hosts who violate the new policy may face warnings, listing removal, or even a ban from the platform. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze states that "reasonable" requests, like putting dirty dishes in the sink, are still permitted.

Some hosts are attempting to find loopholes, such as moving rules to other listing sections or creating "house manuals" with codewords, though many of these methods are either unenforceable or already against existing Airbnb policy.
A call for a platform-wide strike has emerged among some hosts, aiming to send a "powerful message" to Airbnb about who holds the power in their ecosystem.
